strategy_title: Autotune on small kernel causes register explosion and slowdown
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune to a very small kernel (12 blocks, <4 us) caused registers per thread to explode from 34 to 148, collapsing theoretical occupancy from 75% to 18.75% and Block Limit Registers from 12 to 3 blocks/SM. Despite the grid remaining at 12 blocks (autotune did not fix the 2D grid launch because the grid lambda was not updated), executed instructions grew 4.8x (11387 to 54736) and duration nearly doubled (3.78 to 6.34 us). The anti-pattern is applying autotune without also correcting the grid launch expression: the grid stayed 1D=(12,) so the Y-dimension was never populated, yet the autotune overhead and register pressure were fully paid.
slow_pseudocode:
# Before: 1D grid, low register count, no autotune
grid = (cdiv(xnumel, 8),)  # = (12,) — only X dimension
kernel[grid](..., YBLOCK=8, XBLOCK=128)  # 34 registers/thread, 75% theoretical occupancy
applicable_when: Kernel uses program_id(1)/program_id(2) for Y-dimension but grid is launched as 1D; LaunchConfiguration NCU rule fires with >80% speedup estimate; grid_size << sm_count.
do_not_apply_when: Do not add @triton.autotune without simultaneously fixing the grid launch to a 2D/3D lambda that covers all program_id dimensions used in the kernel body. Do not apply autotune to kernels where the total work is tiny (grid_size=12, duration<5us) as autotune overhead and register spill from config exploration can dominate. Avoid when registers per thread are already near the block-limit boundary (34 regs → Block Limit Registers=12; autotune pushed to 148 regs → Block Limit Registers=3).
framework_notes: In Triton, @triton.autotune must be paired with a grid lambda `lambda META: (cdiv(xnumel, META['XBLOCK']), cdiv(ynumel, META['YBLOCK']))` that reads tile sizes from META. A static grid tuple ignores autotune config tile sizes entirely. Autotune also increases register usage due to config-switching overhead; on small kernels this can halve theoretical occupancy.

strategy_title: Fix 1D Grid Missing Y Dimension via Autotune
strategy_description: When a Triton kernel uses tl.program_id(1) and tl.program_id(2) to index a Y dimension but the launch grid is only 1D (e.g., grid=(cdiv(xnumel, XBLOCK),)), program_id(1) and program_id(2) are always 0, so only the first YBLOCK rows are ever processed. The fix is to replace the 1D grid with a 2D grid=(cdiv(xnumel, XBLOCK), cdiv(ynumel, YBLOCK)) and add @triton.autotune to select optimal tile sizes. This reduced elapsed cycles from 5642 to 4325 (23% reduction) and improved theoretical occupancy from 75% to 100% by reducing register pressure from 34 to 32 registers/thread via the autotune-selected configuration.
slow_pseudocode:
# Broken: 1D grid ignores Y dimension entirely
grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 8),)  # = (12,) — pid(1) and pid(2) always 0
kernel[grid](..., YBLOCK=8, XBLOCK=128)  # only first 8 Y rows processed
applicable_when: Triton kernel uses tl.program_id(1) and/or tl.program_id(2) for a Y dimension but the launch grid is 1D (grid=(cdiv(xnumel, XBLOCK),)); NCU LaunchConfiguration rule fires with high speedup_pct (>80%); waves_per_sm is near 0 (e.g., 0.01); achieved occupancy is very low (<10%) despite reasonable theoretical occupancy; grid_size << sm_count.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel genuinely uses only tl.program_id(0) (1D kernel); the low grid size is intentional (e.g., reduction kernel where each block handles a full reduction); the Y dimension is already covered by the 1D grid through a different indexing scheme.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: tl.program_id(0), tl.program_id(1), tl.program_id(2) map to grid dimensions X, Y, Z respectively. A 1D grid tuple (N,) means only program_id(0) varies; program_id(1) and program_id(2) are always 0. The @triton.autotune decorator with key=['ynumel','xnumel'] allows the runtime to select optimal XBLOCK/YBLOCK tile sizes. Also note: changing positional mask argument to keyword mask= argument in tl.load/tl.store is a minor correctness/style fix that does not affect performance.
